title: Unified Physical-Layer Architecture for Next-Generation AGI and Quantum Infrastructure: Integrating Room-Temperature Coherence, Deterministic Interlocks, and Telecommunications Defense
abstract: Abstract: The exponential expansion of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and scalable quantum computing has precipitated a systemic, tri-fold crisis: thermodynamic and cryogenic limits in compute substrates, autonomous governance failures in emergent agentic systems, and structural vulnerabilities in telecommunications infrastructure. Traditional mitigation frameworks remain anchored to software abstraction layers—probabilistic alignment, logical filtering, and protocol-level key exchanges—all of which fail when subjected to hardware saturation, malicious state interception, or adversarial model divergence. This monograph establishes a Unified Physical-Layer Architecture that substitutes software-level heuristics with deterministic hardware controls. First, we resolve the thermodynamic bottleneck of cryogenic dilution refrigeration by formalizing the Adaptive Phonon-Gate and the PHOENIX_BRIDGE architecture, achieving room-temperature quantum spin-photonics integration and coherent state preservation via phononic bandgap manipulation and cavity electro-optics. Second, to govern hyper-autonomous multi-agent swarms under high-entropy electronic warfare (EW) conditions, we formulate Operation SOLID GENESIS and Q-SAFA v2 (Quantum-Secure Automated Fallback Architecture). These frameworks incorporate zero-knowledge Virtual Machine (zkVM) verification directly into optoelectronic circuit breakers and implement non-recoverable physical weight-pruning, establishing hardware-grounded fiduciary compliance aligned with the Delaware Caremark Standard. Finally, we eliminate systemic tracking vulnerabilities inherent in legacy telecommunications through an optically isolated Deterministic Defense Model and continuous subsea cable acoustic-sensing arrays (Project Dawlish). By anchoring thermodynamic equilibrium, algorithmic containment, and telecommunications security to the immutable stratum of physical-layer mechanics, this work provides a non-probabilistic blueprint for sovereign, resilient frontier infrastructure.

title: A multimodal deep learning framework for automated oral English fluency assessment
abstract: The rapid growth in the number of oral English assessments, together with increasing demands for high accuracy and large-scale evaluation, has exposed the limitations of conventional manual scoring systems, which are often subjective, time-consuming, and labor-intensive. This study proposes a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates speech and text features for automated oral English fluency assessment. The model utilizes the Speech Content, Fluency, and Pronunciation Scores dataset obtained from Kaggle, comprising speech recordings, corresponding transcripts, and proficiency annotations, which were divided into training and testing subsets for model development and evaluation. Log-Mel spectrograms are extracted to represent acoustic characteristics, while BERT embeddings capture contextual semantic information from speech transcripts. A self-attention mechanism effectively fuses these multimodal features to evaluate fluency, pronunciation, rhythm, and emotional expression. The framework achieved 97.53% accuracy, 97.68% precision, 97.53% recall, and 97.52% F1-score. Experimental performance was evaluated against conventional single-modal deep learning approaches, demonstrating improved assessment accuracy and robustness. TensorFlow was employed for model training and optimization, whereas PyTorch was utilized for implementing and evaluating transformer-based BERT embeddings, leveraging the strengths of both frameworks within the multimodal pipeline. Integrated structure provides an efficient, scalable, and objective solution for automated oral English fluency assessment across diverse educational environments. The proposed framework incorporates audio data augmentation and ANOVA-based feature selection to improve robustness against accent variations and recording noise.

title: Non-degeneracy and Fibering with Applications to Diophantine Approximation
abstract: Motivated by applications in Diophantine approximation, we develop a new fibering mechanism for non-degenerate manifolds in R^n, showing that they admit local decompositions into families of non-degenerate curves with uniform quantitative non-degeneracy properties. The manifolds are required to be C^N with the essentially optimal bound Ngeq maxlbrace n,l+1rbrace, where the manifold is l non-degenerate. Furthermore, we show that this uniform quantitative local control can be globalised into a qualitative statement, so that almost every point of a non-degenerate manifold lies on a non-degenerate curve contained in the manifold. Our approach is perturbative and shows that the fibering structure arising in the analytic setting is stable under sufficiently small C^N perturbations. The method provides a framework for extending fibering based results in Diophantine approximation from curves to manifolds. Such applications are considered in the paper.

title: Quantum Networking at the Speed of Quantum Computation: Kilohertz Entanglement in a Heterogeneous Quantum System
abstract: Distributed quantum computing requires rapid, high-fidelity entanglement between qubits in separate processor modules. Photonic links between single-atom qubits provide switchable, long-range connections, but photon loss limits their entanglement rate. Here we entangle a trapped $^{138}$Ba$^{+}$ ion with a silicon-vacancy (SiV$^{-}$) center in a diamond nanophotonic cavity. A photon emitted by the ion is converted in wavelength and encoding, reflected from the SiV$^{-}$--cavity system and detected, so that a single detected photon heralds entanglement. Including all conversion losses, we generate ion--SiV$^{-}$ Bell pairs at an average rate of 1.03(1) kHz with a fidelity of 87.9(7)%. This is four times the rate of the fastest photonic link between two trapped ions and corresponds to one Bell pair per millisecond, matching the cycle time of planned trapped-ion processors.

title: Self-Organization from Constrained Geometric Radiation
abstract: How does dynamic order emerge spontaneously in closed systems without external driving? Existing paradigms all require external energy flows, temperature quenching, or slow driving. Here we report constraint-induced self-organization via geometric radiation in coupled metric evolution systems. Simulations reveal a universal four-stage cycle: stress accumulation, super-exponential radiation, chaotic collapse, and convergence to a fractal limit cycle, a novel attractor topology we term the wedge-shaped attractor, with five quantized curvature states and fractal micro-fluctuations. We identify four jointly sufficient conditions: an irreversible geometric horizon, persistent stress injection from quantum coherence, endogenous geometric tension between incompatible curvatures, and effective fluctuations. Their synergy triggers a critical avalanche at the horizon boundary. We prove three theorems: the Geometric Horizon Theorem, the Geometric Energy Dissipation Theorem (implying wave-like entropy evolution in closed systems), and the Radiation as Phase Transition Channel Theorem. We further establish the Constraint-Induced Self-Organization Theorem: these conditions guarantee the complete cycle with probability one. Systematic scans reveal a critical noise threshold and power-law scaling of radiation onset. We verify universality across 12 configurations, multiple noise types, and three geometric flows. This work establishes a new paradigm for closed-system self-organization, forging an exact mathematical duality between classical nonlinear constraints and gravitational horizons.

title: Universal Local Error and Realized Amplification for the First-Order EDM Predictor
abstract: We analyze the first-order deterministic diffusion sampler of Karras et al. (2022), termed EDM, in 2-Wasserstein distance by separating two sources of error: local discretization error and its amplification by subsequent learned steps. We prove that local error admits a universal bound: for any data distribution with finite second moment, the one-step discretization error is quadratic in the step size, with an explicit constant that does not depend on the data distribution. Error propagation, in contrast, depends on the learned network. At high noise levels, we exploit the network parametrization of EDM to derive an explicit contraction criterion. At low noise levels, we measure propagation through the amplification realized on the distributions transported by the sampler; this realized amplification can be arbitrarily smaller than the worst-case Lipschitz constant. This analysis yields an $O(e^{Λ_K}/K)$ global discretization error for $K$ sampling steps, where $Λ_K$ is the low-noise log-amplification. Experiments on a one-dimensional Gaussian mixture show how measured amplification accounts for slower error decay on finite sampling grids. Diagnostics on a pretrained CIFAR-10 model illustrate related stability mechanisms without certifying the global assumptions.

title: Beyond Nominal Equilibria: Risk-Averse Multi-Population Mean-Field Games
abstract: Recent advances in mean-field games and its multi-population variants enable large-scale heterogeneous multi-agent systems to be modeled through representative agents and their associated mean-field distributions. However, existing approaches do not explicitly account for uncertainty in the behavior of other populations. To this end, we introduce a new paradigm: risk-averse multi-population mean-field games, where each population optimizes a worst-case expected reward over dynamically feasible ambiguity sets of mean-field flows of a subset of the other populations. Employing an occupation-measure formulation along with tools from set-valued analysis, we establish, under mild assumptions, several theoretical properties of the multi-population game, including the geometric properties of the ambiguity sets and the existence of a novel risk-averse multi-population mean-field equilibrium. Further, we derive contractivity results of the fixed-point operator under entropy regularization and show that it can be utilized to learn the equilibrium. Finally, we propose a risk-averse fictitious-play scheme and show that exploitability decays to zero, despite the additional nonlinearity introduced by the worst-case objective. We report several numerical experiments to illustrate convergence and risk-averse behavior.

title: Antipodal Necessity and the Cubic Case of the Homogeneous Rotation-Symmetric Bent Function Conjecture
abstract: We prove a structural antipodal necessity theorem for low-degree rotation-symmetric bent functions. In every positive even dimension n, if a rotation-symmetric Boolean function f is bent and deg f ≤ 3, then its algebraic normal form contains the antipodal quadratic orbit P_n(x) = sum_{i=0}^{n/2-1} x_i x_{i+n/2}. As an immediate consequence, no homogeneous rotation-symmetric Boolean function of algebraic degree three is bent in any positive even dimension, settling the cubic case of the homogeneous rotation-symmetric bent-function conjecture. The proof is algebraic and uniform in the dimension. Writing n = 2^s m with m odd, we first transfer bentness to the fixed space of the odd-order rotation σ^{2^s}. In the resulting power-of-two dimension, a fiber argument forces the antipodal orbit. An exact orbit-folding formula then transports its coefficient back to the original dimension. No computational classification is used.

title: K501 Information Space: Proof-Bound Temporal Memory Infrastructure for Machine Cognition
abstract: Version 0.1 of the K501 Information Space research dossier and reproducibility package. This record documents the current research-layer state of the K501 Information Space as a developing proof-bound external memory architecture for artificial intelligence. It consolidates formal system definitions, current implementation and validation evidence, provenance and temporal reconstruction structures, comparative scientific context, reproducibility material, and the remaining open research boundaries. The publication distinguishes between established external scientific foundations, K501-specific specifications, implementation evidence, derived structures, historical material, and open questions. It therefore does not present unresolved architectural or empirical questions as completed results. In particular, the record does not claim that K501 has already solved general artificial memory, truth, hallucination, distributed consensus, or production-scale agent control. The accompanying research package contains the publication dossier and the associated reproducibility materials, including machine-readable metadata, evidence and proof material, references, reference code, checksums, reproduction information, and development-roadmap material. The package is intended to make the stated research state inspectable and reproducible without replacing the canonical K501, QH256, or eArc repositories. The dossier represents the research state at Unix time anchor 1791400380 (2026-10-07 19:13:00 UTC / 21:13:00 CEST). It is a research-layer consolidation and does not supersede the earlier QH256 scientific publication, QH256 repository, or other canonical project repositories. The record should therefore be understood as a versioned scientific research artifact documenting a bounded state of development rather than as a declaration of a completed general-purpose memory system.

title: 全球矿产勘探"财富密码" 2026:全球、澳大利亚与中国一线矿产勘探热点排行榜
abstract: 💰 哪里正在找矿?哪里最热?哪里可能藏着下一座大矿? 如果你想寻找全球矿产勘探的“财富密码”,第一步可能不是研究某一家矿业公司,而是先看看: 钱正在往哪里投,钻机正在往哪里开,勘探人员正在往哪里跑。 本数据集整理了三张矿产勘探热点排行榜,分别从全球、澳大利亚和中国三个尺度,对当前值得重点关注的一线矿产勘探区域、矿产区、成矿带、资源节点和勘探热点进行整理。 本数据集包含三个核心表格 1. 全球一线矿产勘探热度排行榜 🌍 整理全球重要矿产勘探热点,包括主要国家、矿产区、成矿带、核心城市/节点、主要矿种以及区域勘探意义。 重点关注全球矿产勘探资本、钻探活动、重大矿产发现和资源前沿地区。 2. 澳大利亚一线矿产勘探排行榜 🇦🇺 澳大利亚是全球最重要的矿产勘探市场之一。本表重点整理西澳、昆士兰、南澳、新南威尔士、北领地、维多利亚和塔斯马尼亚的重要勘探区、矿田、地质省和资源节点。 涉及金、铜、铁矿石、锂、镍、铅锌、稀土等主要矿种及其重要勘探区域。 3. 中国一线矿产勘探热门榜 🇨🇳 整理中国重要矿产资源省区、成矿带、矿集区和勘探热点,重点关注金属矿产、能源矿产以及战略性矿产资源。 为什么做这个表? 因为矿产勘探说到底是一场**“地质 + 资本 + 时间 + 地理位置”的游戏**。 一个优秀的地质师或地球物理工程师,当然需要技术能力。 但如果你恰好位于: 一个优秀的成矿带 + 一个正在获得大量勘探资本的地区 + 一个正在高速增长的矿种市场 你的职业机会、项目规模和未来收入,都可能发生完全不同的变化。 所以这三张表可以被理解为一份非常不严肃、但又很认真的: 🌍⛏️ 全球矿产勘探藏宝图 当然,如果按照最不严肃的理解: 找到热点 → 找到矿 → 找到老板 → 买大别墅。 现实中的地质学显然不会这么配合。🤣 真正严肃的版本则是: 想研究矿产资源的未来,先研究勘探资本和勘探活动正在往哪里走。 本数据集不构成投资建议,也不是矿产资源量/储量估算,更不能保证任何地区未来一定发现大型矿床。 它更适合作为矿产勘探、经济地质、地球物理、采矿工程、资源产业研究、矿业投资研究以及国际矿业职业规划的区域导航资料。 大矿是真的,钱也是真的。至于能不能靠它住上大别墅,心动不如行动!💰🏠⛏️

title: Clustering trajectories of modelled estimates: uncertainty aware trajectory clustering code and data
abstract: v1.0.0: Uncertainty-aware trajectory clustering of modelled estimates First public release of the R code that accompanies the manuscript on clustering country trajectories of Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 estimates, with cardiovascular disease (CVD) as the case study. What it does Separates each country's trajectory into level and shape (mean-centred log rates) and clusters the shapes with Ward's method. Propagates the published uncertainty intervals into the clustering by value perturbation, giving each country a membership probability $p_i$. Assigns countries only when $p_i \ge 0.70$ and selects the number of clusters as the largest $k$ whose weakest cluster has a median $p_i \ge 0.80$. Compares the result with silhouette, gap statistic and a country bootstrap, and examines spatial autocorrelation (Moran's $I$) and the correlates of membership (SDI, super region, interval width). Contents | Path | Purpose | |---|---| | R/framework.R | Core functions: shape decomposition, clustering, stability, $k$ selection, Moran's $I$, helpers | | analysis/01_run_analysis.R | Main analysis; writes Figures 1 to 8, Figure S1 and Tables 1 to 5 | | analysis/02_supplement_tables.R | Supplementary Tables S1 to S7 | | data/ | GBD 2023 extracts (CVD DALYs and deaths, SDI), super region and income group lookups, reference membership | | tests/test_reproduction.R | Checks the reproduced partition and membership probabilities against the reference | | run_all.sh | Runs the full pipeline and the test | Reproducing ./run_all.sh Requires R 4.3 or later with cluster, nnet and maps. Seed 20261003; B = 1000 perturbation replicates (set GBD_B to change). Runs in about two minutes on a standard laptop. sessionInfo.txt records the environment used; GitHub Actions reruns the pipeline on every push. Licence and data Code is released under the MIT licence. GBD data are used under the IHME Free of Charge Non-commercial User Agreement; cite IHME and the GBD 2023 publications when reusing them. Citation See CITATION.cff. Please cite the accompanying manuscript once published.

title: Copyright Law and Artificial Intelligence: Current U.S. Regulation, Ethical Considerations, and Impact on Licensing Trends
abstract: This presentation overviewed interactions between United States (U.S.) copyright law and artificial intelligence (AI). In recent years, extensive economic activity around AI surfaced new business-oriented issues, including new copyright issues. Throughout 2023 and 2024, the U.S. Copyright Office held listening sessions around generative AI and copyright, and is now releasing guidance. A current parallel regulatory thrust is comprehensive U.S. federal regulation of AI. The National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act (NAIIA) of 2020 provided funding for a five-year rollout of AI regulation, including AI ethics. With AI ethics regulation in rapid development in the U.S., and legally binding outcomes pending, large corporations building AI tools have a strong incentive to control the conversation and define AI ethics. By emphasizing copyright, large corporations might seek to shift emphasis away from ethical issues

title: Can the Quantum Fisher Effective Dimension Judge a Hybrid Quantum Neural Network?
abstract: Hybrid quantum neural networks (QNNs) pair a classical feature extractor with a variational quantum circuit, and the effective dimension of the circuit's quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) is widely used to assess such models. This scalar is often interpreted as an indicator of trainability or accuracy, although these readings are rarely tested under controlled conditions. We therefore investigate what it actually measures. We define the effective dimension as the participation ratio of the QFIM diagonal, which lies between one and the parameter count, and we evaluate it across two image datasets, four frozen backbones including a random-projection control, four circuit depths on eight qubits, and three seeds. During training, the effective dimension remains well below the parameter count, and its correlation with test accuracy ranges from -0.72 to +0.87, changing sign across seeds in half of the configurations. Increasing depth activates a larger share of the circuit directions, from 0.38 to 0.91 of the parameter count, while the initialization gradient variance remains between 1e-5 and 1e-4, so no barren plateau (BP) appears at eight qubits. At a fixed circuit, the four backbones share an initial effective dimension of 6 to 9, even though CIFAR-10 accuracy ranges from 23.14% to 86.44%. These results show that the effective dimension characterizes circuit geometry rather than model quality. We conclude with a practical protocol that assigns each diagnostic to the question it can answer.

title: KDFP: A first-principles approach to knowledge distillation in large language models
abstract: Knowledge distillation is an established technique for improving the capabilities of small, efficient student models by training them with the representations of larger, more capable teacher models. Much of the recent work in the distillation of large language models (LLMs) has focused on distilling abilities learned during post-training, such as instruction following, chain-of-thought reasoning, and tool usage. This has left a large research gap in general knowledge distillation for LLMs, which is essential for developing efficient and private systems suitable for deployment on edge devices. We take a first-principles approach, evaluating previous lessons from prior works and conducting new explorations to develop a distillation methodology suitable for modern LLMs. We present KDFP, a novel methodology for white-box general knowledge distillation in LLMs. We demonstrate that KDFP outperforms existing methods by 1.6% $-$ 4.9% across 9 benchmarks while increasing training efficiency by up to 99.1% through ephemeral parameter reduction.

title: Beyond gauge-parameter dependence: Further evidence for asymptotic safety in Scalar-Tensor theories
abstract: Asymptotic Safety provides a promising framework for the quantization of Scalar-Tensor theories as non-perturbatively renormalizable quantum field theories. Over the past years, growing evidence has accumulated for the existence of non-trivial renormalization group fixed points in a variety of Scalar-Tensor models. In this work, we investigate the robustness of these fixed points under significant modifications of the computational setup. In particular, we employ a gauge condition that explicitly depends on the dynamical scalar field, going beyond a mere gauge-parameter deformation of the standard linear covariant gauges commonly used in the literature. Exploring different field parameterizations, we identify fixed points belonging to the Gaussian Matter class in four spacetime dimensions that are consistent with previous studies. The real part of the critical exponents associated with the scalar-field mass and the non-minimal scalar-curvature coupling turn out to have very small absolute value. We provide a comprehensive exploration of how the anomalous dimension of the scalar field and field parameterization impact those critical exponents showing that fixed-point candidates with two or four relevant directions emerge.

title: Kinetic Langevin Meets Split Gibbs: Accelerated Posterior Sampling for Imaging Inverse Problems with Diffusion Priors
abstract: Split Gibbs sampling (SGS) is a popular framework for posterior sampling in Bayesian imaging inverse problems. It decouples a Gaussian data-fidelity term from a complex prior through an auxiliary variable, so the data variable is updated exactly and only the prior-side conditional is hard to sample. Existing samplers treat this conditional in one of two ways. Plug-and-play SGS runs a multi-step diffusion denoiser at every iteration, which is expensive and lacks non-asymptotic guarantees. Langevin-within-SGS takes cheap overdamped Langevin steps but needs many iterations. We propose RED-KLwSGS, which keeps the exact Gaussian update for the data variable and updates the auxiliary variable with underdamped (kinetic) Langevin diffusions driven by a one-shot denoising score, at the same per-iteration cost as Langevin-within-SGS. We prove non-asymptotic Wasserstein-2 convergence in continuous and discrete time for strongly log-concave priors. We also introduce Joint-RED-KLwSGS, which applies kinetic Langevin diffusions to both variables. Experiments with Denoising diffusion probabilistic models as diffusion priors on FFHQ and ImageNet datasets show faster convergence and high-quality image reconstruction.

title: Axial-metric/polar-gauge perturbations of the Maldacena-Milekhin-Popov wormhole
abstract: We study linear perturbations of the Maldacena-Milekhin-Popov (MMP) wormhole in the parity sector that pairs axial metric perturbations with polar gauge perturbations. It contains the axial gravitational mode and the electric field along the magnetic field lines. The lowest Landau level (LLL) of the charged fermions responds through its charge. The gauge components a_τ, a_ρ form a two-dimensional gauge field on the worldsheet of each field line, and the fermions respond with the exact Schwinger current. Lifted over the sphere, it gives the electric field the MMP screening mass m_S^2=αq^2, which is not small and survives in the mouth. In the throat the perturbation tilts the worldsheets, and the Casimir stress tensor acquires mixed components. Force balance then requires a current across the field lines, and charge conservation fixes an accompanying polarisation current, the counterpart of the Hall current of the polar sector. These currents close the Bianchi identities at first order in the fermionic backreaction α. The system reduces to three coupled master equations, given in closed form and matched to the fermion-free mouth. Consistency alone does not select the fermionic constitutive relation, but locality, covariance and the index theorem do. At α=0 the throat reduces to Poschl-Teller problems with masses l(l-1) and (l+1)(l+2) at m_S^2=0. At finite m_S^2 one mode is screened, one tends to the mass l^2+l+2, and one neutral charge-density wave stays exactly massless. The O(α) shifts of the massive normal frequencies are real and negative. The two parity sectors are isospectral only without fermions. The neutral channel sees an attractive region in each mouth, and a numerical solution coupled to the gravitational channel in the exact mouth potential finds no bound state. The sector has no growing mode for lge2 at this order.

title: Anchor Is the Key —Anchoring is the Premise of Attention, and the First Bridge of the Dual-Subject AI Architecture
abstract: "Attention Is All You Need" defined the starting point of the Transformer: the attention mechanism replaced recurrence and convolution as the sole core of sequence modeling. But it left one question unasked: why does attention work? This paper offers an intuitive answer: because of the anchor. Without an anchor, computation is wasted in repetition; with an anchor, attention can be reused over a determined history and computed on a stable foundation. The core claim of this paper can be compressed into a single verifiable statement: scheduling tools inside the decoding loop and appending results at the tail can reduce repeated Prefill from O(M×N) to O(N+M·K) while preserving the prefix KV. This claim is developed on three levels. Mathematical level (intuitive mapping): the anchor is the condition of a conditional probability; anchored Attention is the engineering realization of conditional probability. Information-theoretic level: the anchor is already-compressed information; anchoring means freezing the compressed part and compressing only the newly added information. Philosophical level: the anchor is the physical expression of probability convergence; the soul is the ability to realize probability cliffs, and the anchor is the engineering projection of the cliff. This paper further proposes the Anchoring Paradigm: general deterministic capabilities sink to the engine layer; results are appended at the tail during streaming generation; the KV Cache hits 100%; the anchor is never lost. The Agent layer handles only vertical business relations. This is the conceptual unfolding of the "Dual-Subject AI Architecture": the Engine is the anchored general subject; the Agent is the changing vertical relation. Finally, this paper draws the Anchor Map—marking, at every critical node of the AI lifecycle, where an anchor can be set. This is a declaration of sovereignty: not "the anchor is here," but "the anchor can be here."

title: Kanakkathigaram-NLP: A Bilingual Tamil–English Dataset of Classical Arithmetic Problems (v2)
abstract: This dataset is derived from the Kanakkathigaram, a classical Tamil arithmetic text traditionally attributed to Karinayanar, as compiled in the critical edition published by the Saraswathi Mahal Library, Thanjavur (Publication No. 388, edited by Sathiyaparama Kameswaran, first edition September 1998). It supports NLP research on mathematical reasoning in a low-resource classical language setting, and includes the full bilingual problem set, a traditional measurement (alavai) glossary, a classical numeral fraction (pinna ilakkam) reference, and step-by-step reasoning chains. Changes in v2: Recovered 15 problems that were structurally merged into adjacent records in v1 due to source-file boundary errors (199 → 214 total problems) Replaced the non-unique book chapter-numbering scheme with globally unique record identifiers (uid); the original book numbering is retained as a non-key reference field (book_number) Corrected multiple wrong symbol-to-value mappings for classical Tamil fraction notation (pinna ilakkam), verified against an authoritative reference table Fixed a script-encoding error (Malayalam characters erroneously present in place of Tamil in two records) Added a dedicated, verified fraction/numeral reference file (previously undocumented) Restructured the dataset from mixed-language single files into six purpose-separated files, each with consistent Tamil/English and Tamil-numeral/Roman-numeral conventions Files: kanakkathigaram_v2_tamil_problems.jsonl — 214 problems in Tamil, original verse/commentary form, Tamil numerals preserved kanakkathigaram_v2_english_problems.jsonl — parallel English translations with worked solutions, Roman numerals kanakkathigaram_v2_alavai_glossary.jsonl — 155 traditional measurement-unit conversion records (land, grain, currency, length) kanakkathigaram_v2_karinayanar_voice.jsonl — 89 Q&A records in the traditional poetic register attributed to Karinayanar kanakkathigaram_v2_reasoning_chains.jsonl — 53 paired bilingual step-by-step derivation records kanakkathigaram_v2_pinna_ilakkam_fractions.jsonl — 35 records defining the classical Tamil fractional numeral system (symbol, value, decimal equivalent, name)

title: Raell's Revocation Indistinguishability Theorem: External Eligibility Is Necessary for Record Invalidation
abstract: We prove that no revocation mechanism whose input is entirely determined by the store's own state can decide revocation authority with respect to an external eligibility oracle. The result is the second instance of the pattern established in Raell's Rollback Indistinguishability Theorem (2026): the ground cannot be found in the grounded. We scope the theorem to O-agnostic states, states that contain no value cryptographically bound to the external authority O, which covers retained bytes, local tombstones, and local revocation flags uniformly. A lemma separates authenticity of the revocation tag from authority of the revocation, refuting the objection that a MAC suffices. Three machine-checked artifacts accompany the theorem: a bounded finite-model check, an SMT conformance test, and a Lean 4 formalization of the deterministic core. We state the verification tier discipline explicitly in Section 10. The result names and characterizes the storage-layer gap identified by the "Revoked but Still Authoritative" finding (Sept 2026).

title: Optimization of a 942-Bar Tower Truss Structure Using Metaheuristics
abstract: Truss structures are fundamental components in civil/structural engineering design, characterized by their lightweight and load-bearing capabilities. This chapter aims to compare the effectiveness of three metaheuristics, namely the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), the Evaporation Rate-based Water Cycle Algorithm (ERWCA), and the Gaze Cues Learning-based Grey Wolf Optimizer (GGWO) in achieving an optimal design configuration that minimizes the truss’s weight while satisfying structural constraints. The chosen optimization problem in this chapter is a 26-story structural truss having 942 bars. The comparative results of the minimum objective function value (structural weight) and the computational efficiency to reach the optimal solutions are evaluated using optimization simulations. From the findings, the GGWO shows its superiority among the three metaheuristics in terms of the quality of the solution based on both the best achieved minimum value of the objective function and the average of minimum values over 30 optimization simulation runs at the expense of slower convergence rate than the other two metaheuristics. 96 This research underscores the importance of employing metaheuristics for complex engineering optimization tasks. It provides a basis for further exploration of metaheuristics’ application in other complex and challenging engineering design systems in the pursuit of improved solution quality and convergence rates.

title: From Hitter to Player: Separating Motor Execution and Strategy in Competitive Humanoid Table Tennis
abstract: Competitive humanoid table tennis requires two distinct abilities: executing a desired return and deciding where to return the ball. We separate these two problems, with the ball landing target serving as an interface between motor control and strategy. (1) We first train a whole-body motor policy conditioned on the desired landing target, which maps the target to an executable humanoid stroke through a model-based strike planner and a learned controller. (2) We then improve the motor policy through self-play in closed-loop rallies, where the robot learns to handle incoming balls generated by another player rather than only prescribed incoming balls. At this stage, the landing targets are still sampled without considering the opponent, so the policy improves its execution without learning game strategy. (3) Finally, we freeze the entire motor stack and train a stroke-level strategic policy to choose landing targets through competitive self-play. Motor self-play improves both landing accuracy and legal-return rate during rallies. More importantly, with the entire motor stack fixed, changing only the target-selection policy leads to large differences in game outcomes: the learned strategy wins 89%, 82%, and 73% of points against center, random, and away-from-opponent baselines, respectively. The learned strategy also changes where it sends the ball according to the opponent's position and the previous target, showing that self-play learns more than simply aiming at fixed "good" locations. On hardware, the same frozen execution stack and strategic interface support complete 11-point games against a recreational human opponent, including multi-stroke rallies with both forehand and backhand returns.

title: Similar Predictive Fit but Different Latent Dynamics: Characterizing Learned Dynamical Structure in Personalized Models of Brain Disorders
abstract: As AI models move toward clinical decision-making and personalized treatment, understanding \emph{what} a model learns is important beyond predictive accuracy alone. We investigate whether personalized latent dynamics reveal clinically associated differences even when predictive fit is similar. A lightweight CNN--Transformer EEG foundation model pretrained on the Temple University EEG Corpus (TUEG) extracts segment-level representations. Using the Temple University Epilepsy Corpus (TUEP), representations are mapped to a shared latent-state space, and sparse multinomial logistic transition distributions (mLTD) are fit independently to each subject to obtain personalized transition-dependency graphs $W_n$. Analyses include $n{=}198$ subjects (99 epilepsy / 99 non-epilepsy). At $k{=}4$, epilepsy subjects exhibit substantially denser learned dependency structure ($p{=}1.1\times10^{-7}$), with the same pattern at $k{=}6$ (19.90 vs. 13.46; $p{=}5.2\times10^{-5}$). Graph-derived features provide moderate group discrimination under 5-fold subject-wise cross-validation (AUROC 0.68 at $k{=}4$; 0.65 at $k{=}6$). In contrast, held-out log-likelihood is nearly identical between groups at $k{=}4$ ($-0.992$ vs. $-0.991$; $p{=}0.95$), with similarly matched next-state prediction (AUROC 0.855 vs. 0.861; $p{=}0.54$). Thus, similar predictive fit does not imply similar learned dynamics: groups can be comparably predictable while differing substantially in the internal dynamical structure learned by personalized models. This distinction motivates evaluating learned structure alongside predictive performance in personalized clinical models.

title: Safe Meta-Policy Design with Risk Control
abstract: Models can be retrained as new data arrive, but deploying every new version risks replacing a good policy with a worse one. We study how to plan policy updates (i.e., meta-policy) before future candidates are trained, balancing the benefits of improvement against the risk of performance regression. Our offline meta-policy maximizes expected cumulative value subject to a budget on the expected number of updates that perform worse than the policies they replace. We estimate the value and risk of possible switches from historical learning trajectories, represent an update schedule as a path in a directed acyclic graph, and select a schedule using dynamic programming. A leading-order analysis identifies the signal-to-noise ratio of policy improvement as a key driver of update frequency, waiting times, and risk allocation: clearer improvements support earlier, more frequent updates, while noisier improvements call for longer waits or greater risk expenditure. Their asymptotic rates also reveal a diminishing marginal cost of achieving greater safety over time. Experiments on synthetic and clinical trial data illustrate the performance--risk tradeoff and compare our method with alternative baselines.

title: Pre-training of Bayesian Optimization Algorithm through Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used as a standard approach for expensive black-box optimization. However, BO algorithms often involve parameters that must be specified in advance, and their performance can strongly depend on these choices. We propose a framework for optimizing such parameters using sample paths drawn from a Gaussian process (GP) inferred from the information available at the start of BO. We use cumulative regret as the performance metric for a BO algorithm. By running the BO algorithm on the generated sample paths, we obtain an empirical estimate of its expected cumulative regret for a given parameter configuration. Optimizing this estimate allows us to identify parameter configurations that, given the currently available information, are expected to achieve low cumulative regret. Since this parameter optimization is itself a black-box optimization problem, we employ another BO procedure to solve it, which we refer to as outer BO. Through experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed framework can effectively select parameter configurations that achieve strong performance among a range of candidate configurations.

title: Constrained-Action AI Remediation for SIEM/XDR via a NeMo-Guardrails Proxy
abstract: Security Operations Centers (SOCs) for information technology and operational technology share one incident-response problem: a flood of correlated alerts and too few analysts. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as reasoning engines that triage alerts and, in autonomous deployments, issue commands that block IPs, kill processes, or quarantine files on production hosts. This coupling introduces a new risk: a single adversarial alert can become a remote code path through the LLM's reasoning, leading it to recommend an action the SOC then executes. We present a constrained-action architecture with two coordinated layers: (i) a SIEM/XDR control plane that grounds remediation in correlated host events and confines the LLM's output to a closed intent vocabulary whose templated commands are executed by thin endpoint agents, backstopped by an argument validator; and (ii) a NeMo-Guardrails proxy that wraps the SOC-analyst LLM with input- and output-rail policies, evaluated out-of-the-box against a SOC-specific adversarial corpus we release. The stock proxy lifts injection recall from 25.0% to 94.5% at a 0.1% false-positive rate, and a live red-team exercise confirms that the closed intent vocabulary and argument validator contain the observed LLM failure modes before any command crosses the trust boundary. As an architectural fit (not yet a measured operational-technology deployment), the constrained-action property suits critical-infrastructure settings where a wrong remediation has physical, not merely operational, consequences. The loop is best run human-in-the-loop or delayed: the measured rail latency keeps inline control out of scope.

title: InstiAct: An Executable Institutional Layer for Agent-Based and Computational Modeling — From Agreement Structures to Dynamic Action Spaces
abstract: This research-software note introduces InstiAct v0.4.6, an independent Python framework for representing institutional admissibility and institutional state transitions in computational models. The note develops the modeling proposition that institutional structures can be represented as an explicit, inspectable, and experimentally variable state that filters candidate actions and can itself change through institutional events. It defines the boundary between institutional admissibility and physical feasibility, operational constraints, behavioral choice, learning, and optimization; documents the executable semantics of rights, hard constraints, defeasible norms, contracts, amendments, remedies, and transactions; and describes the interface for coupling InstiAct to agent-based models. DAMMAGE is treated as an explicit intellectual antecedent for executable rights-and-obligations environments, while InstiAct is positioned conservatively as an independent research implementation rather than a port, reconstruction, or claim of implementation equivalence. The note documents the v0.4.6 software release and supports reproducible computational experiments on institutional dynamics and changing action spaces.

DAMMAGE is treated as an explicit intellectual antecedent for executable rights-and-obligations environments, while InstiAct is positioned conservatively as an independent research implementation rather than a port, reconstruction, or claim of implementation equivalence. The note documents the v0.4.6 software release and supports reproducible computational experiments on institutional dynamics and changing action spaces.

title: Federated Learning for Privacy-Preserving ECG Arrhythmia Classification under Non-IID Data Distributions: A Preliminary Study
abstract: Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of mortality worldwide, and early detection of arrhythmias via electrocardiogram (ECG) analysis is critical for effective intervention. Centralized machine learning approaches for ECG classification require aggregating sensitive patient data, raising significant privacy concerns. Federated Learning (FL) offers a promising alternative by enabling collaborative model training without exchanging raw data. Yet, real-world clinical data across hospitals is inherently non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) due to demographic variation, equipment differences, and local disease prevalence. This paper presents a preliminary empirical study of FL for ECG arrhythmia classification under controlled non-IID conditions. Using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, we simulate five hospital clients partitioned with Dirichlet distributions (α ∈ {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}) and compare Federated Averaging (FedAvg) and Federated Proximal (FedProx) using a compact 1D CNN with class-weighted loss. Our results reveal two findings: (i) both algorithms collapse under severe non-IID (α=0.1), achieving macro F1 ≈ 0.22 while never predicting minority classes; and (ii) under moderate heterogeneity (α=0.5), FedProx outperforms FedAvg by 4.1 percentage points (F1 = 0.617 vs. 0.575), but reverses under milder heterogeneity (α=1.0), where FedAvg leads (F1 = 0.569 vs. 0.493). This non-monotonic behavior, consistent with recent theoretical observations on the proximal term's regularization effect, is itself a contribution. All code, data partitions, and evaluation scripts are released for full reproducibility.

abstract: The El-Rakhawi Engineering of Comprehensive AI (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23209681) unifies algorithms, hardware, infrastructure, and ethics into one engineering framework. Five parts: (1) Cognitive Core covering Video Language Models, 3D Gaussian Splatting, Embodied AI, Neuromorphic Computing, and Causal Foundation Models; (2) Training Engine with distributed training, ZeRO, model compression, Sovereign Federated Learning, and Quantum-AI Convergence; (3) Silicon Backbone detailing GPU/TPU/NPU architecture, HPC, and Bio-Neuromorphic Computing; (4) Planetary Deployment via Cloud-Edge-Fog, Serverless, AI-Native OS, and Digital Sovereignty; (5) Synthesis with a Conceptual Architectural Blueprint, Ethical Charter, and the Comprehensive AI Efficiency Index (CAIEI). CAIEI mathematically normalizes algorithmic power, infrastructure efficiency, sovereignty, and epistemic wisdom against carbon footprint and privacy violations. Integrates with the entire El-Rakhawi Corpus as its applied engineering layer. Released under Ferial Zayed Humanitarian License.

title: ACN Lists, Prompt Templates and Research Code for Risk-Sensitive Evaluation of Large Language Models for Human-Factors Coding in Aviation Safety Reports
abstract: This archive contains the ACN list, complete prompt templates, and experimental and analysis code associated with the study "Risk-Sensitive Evaluation of Large Language Models for Human-Factors Coding in Aviation Safety Reports". The ACN file identifies 389 NASA ASRS reports and their sample groups: 297 Main reports and 92 Fatigue_Supplement reports. The prompt file includes the three primary templates and the names-only and published-description templates used in the supplementary paired zero-shot comparison. Source attribution and licence information for the reproduced category descriptions are retained in that file. The Code directory contains 13 Python files, a README and a dependency list. The sources cover sample reconstruction, experimental collection, primary and supplementary analyses, recorded-outcome associations and figure generation. Publication-oriented collection and input adapters are clearly identified in the README. These scripts require the study-specific inputs described there; prediction datasets, report narratives and execution logs are not bundled. The archive contains 17 files in the ACN, Prompts and Code directories.

title: A quasi experimental study of robotics based learning and differential development of context specific STEM literacy among primary school students
abstract: Abstract This mixed-method quasi-experimental study examined the effects of robotics-based learning on context-specific STEM literacy among primary school students within the Malaysian Reka Bentuk dan Teknologi (RBT) curriculum. The experimental group ( n = 34) participated in FIRST ® LEGO ® League (FLL)-based intervention, while the control group ( n = 34) received conventional instruction. Quantitative findings showed that the experimental group achieved significantly higher post-test STEM literacy scores, t (66) = 8.43, p < 0.001, with a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 2.04). Within-group analyses indicated substantial improvement in the experimental group from pre-test to post-test, t (33) = 15.72, p < 0.001 ( d = 2.69), compared with smaller gains in the control group, t (33) = 7.14, p < 0.001 ( d = 1.22). Domain-level results indicated variation in the magnitude of improvement, with larger effects in programming symbol recognition ( d = 1.87) and programming interface and hardware recognition ( d = 1.69) than in pseudocode construction ( d = 1.24) and flowchart-based problem solving ( d = 0.83). Qualitative findings indicated that students could execute robotics tasks effectively but struggled to translate these experiences into abstract symbolic representations. The study extends robotics-based STEM learning literature by demonstrating differentiated domain-specific effects in the development of context-specific STEM literacy in primary education.

title: Context engineering frames prompt engineering within system level orchestration for large language model applications
abstract: Abstract By moving from isolated instruction crafting to system-level contextual orchestration, context engineering reframes how large language model (LLM) applications are designed for complex, multi-source workflows. Prompt engineering can deliver strong results for narrow, single-turn tasks, yet it often becomes brittle and costly to maintain as interaction length, tool use, governance constraints, and reliability requirements increase. In this perspective, context engineering is used as a working systems concept for the design and governance of context pipelines that determine how relevant data, tool outputs, memory cues, and policy constraints are selected, transformed, structured, validated, and delivered to the model. The term is positioned relative to adjacent paradigms rather than presented as a new model class. Retrieval-augmented generation is treated as a mechanism for context acquisition, tool-augmented reasoning as a mechanism for context creation via external actions, and memory services as a mechanism for context persistence. On this basis, the paper identifies recurring patterns in system design, including dynamic context assembly, token budgeting and compaction, multimodal context composition, memory management, provenance management, and observability. Issues related to anticipated modes of failure include context drift, provenance loss, privacy disclosure, and evaluation instability. The paper argues that system-level context control becomes increasingly important for LLMs when their applications are multi-turn, tool-using, policy-constrained, and provenance-sensitive.

title: Safety-Oriented Trajectory Ranking from BEV Perception Outputs
abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) representations are increasingly used as compact inputs for autonomous driving perception and planning. However, lightweight and interpretable methods for evaluating candidate ego trajectories directly on BEV outputs remain useful for vehicular safety workflows, rapid prototyping, and human-in-the-loop validation. This paper presents a modular trajectory ranking pipeline that consumes BEVFusion object detections and map segmentations derived from nuScenes sensor data and ranks manually specified candidate trajectories according to safety-first criteria. The ranking prioritizes avoiding collisions and walkway violations, then smaller end distance to the target, and finally path efficiency. To study whether these rule-based rankings resemble human judgment, we created seven BEV traffic scenarios and compared the script output with preferences from a survey of 21 participants. Across 146 pairwise votes, 124 matched the trajectory ranked first by the evaluator, corresponding to an overall agreement of 84.9 %. The results indicate that simple BEV-centric safety heuristics can approximate human preferences in constrained trajectory choice tasks while remaining transparent enough for analysis, dataset curation, and autonomous driving studies.

title: Do My Samples Help? Compute Budget Allocation for Real-World Sampling-Based MPC in Contact-Rich Manipulation
abstract: Sampling-based model predictive control (SMPC) is increasingly practical for contact-rich manipulation because GPU-based physics simulators enable real-time evaluation of large numbers of non-differentiable contact rollouts. However, this computation budget is finite and can be spent in competing ways, including denser control exploration, representing dynamics or state uncertainty, replanning more frequently, or aligning the simulation better with the physical state. Yet, the resulting trade-offs are not well understood in real-world sim-to-real control. In this work, we address this question through a systematic study of how to allocate a fixed computation budget for SMPC in contact-rich manipulation. To enable controlled comparisons, we develop a GPU-based framework named Budget-Allocating Model Predictive Control (BAMPC), which runs on MuJoCo Warp and exposes dynamics uncertainty, state uncertainty, and temporal alignment as independent dimensions of the computation budget while using the same control stack in simulation and on a real robot. Across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, we find that the best budget allocation depends on the dominant sim-to-real error, with dynamics randomization not universally the most effective one.

title: Amortized Off-Policy Evaluation for LLMs
abstract: Accurate evaluation is central to selecting which LLM to deploy, yet testing a candidate on live traffic exposes real users to an unvetted model. Teams therefore evaluate candidates offline, on data produced by already-deployed models. This is off-policy evaluation (OPE), and it faces two distribution shifts: as a model is updated in post-training, its responses diverge from the logged ones (policy shift), and the reward definition under which it is judged changes with business requirements (reward shift). Classical OPE methods are ill-suited to this continual-deployment setting because they are defined per task and require fitting from scratch on every new logged dataset or reward definition. To address this, we propose PFN-OPE, a prior-data fitted network that amortizes OPE across a distribution of contextual-bandit tasks. We pretrain it once on tasks constructed from a pool of LLM responses scored by several reward functions, in which both shifts occur. At test-time it maps a logged dataset and one sampled target response per prompt to a value estimate in a single forward pass, with no per-task fitting. On HelpSteer2 and UltraFeedback with Qwen, Llama, and Gemma policies, PFN-OPE achieves 2.0 to 9.3 times lower error than the best baselines across all tested configurations in the reward-shifted settings.

title: K-moduli wall crossing for quasimaps to a projective variety
abstract: We develop a modular wall crossing theory for quasimaps to a projective variety, allowing independent variation of the boundary coefficients and the quasimap weight. Building on the K-stability of quasimaps introduced by Hashizume and the first author, we construct projective moduli spaces in the stable, Calabi--Yau, and log Fano regimes, together with wall crossing morphisms. A central construction is the moduli theory of boundary polarized Calabi--Yau quasimaps, which retains an ample polarization at the numerically trivial locus and allows comparison with suitable perturbations toward the stable and log Fano regions. The stable theory applies in arbitrary genus, while the comparisons through the Calabi--Yau locus concern genus zero. For degree-one boundary divisors, the resulting framework relates weighted stable maps and quasimaps to Hassett spaces and GIT quotients of weighted points on mathbb P^1. In a companion paper, we apply this framework to give a modular interpolation between Miranda's GIT compactification of rational elliptic surfaces and the Baily--Borel compactification of an eight-dimensional ball quotient.

title: MOTIP2: Spatial Priors for End-to-End Multi-Object Tracking
abstract: End-to-end multi-object trackers have narrowed the gap with classical tracking-by-detection on association-difficult benchmarks. Yet they still make spatially implausible errors no classical tracker would, such as assigning one identity to objects on opposite sides of the frame. A model could learn to avoid them, but tracking annotations are scarce, so we encode spatial priors explicitly instead, while keeping inference fully end-to-end with no post-hoc association. We propose three spatial priors, at the data, loss, and representation stages. Spatial ID Switches bias trajectory permutations toward spatially overlapping objects, reducing the mismatch between training and inference confusions. Spatial ID Loss scales each identity's penalty by its box distance, so a distant switch costs more than a nearby one. Spatial Anchor gives each track token its frame position, an explicit spatial cue for attention. We instantiate the three priors in MOTIP2, a tracker adapted from MOTIP and built on the real-time DEIM detection transformer. Trained without extra data, its main model, MOTIP2-L, sets a new state of the art: 73.4 HOTA on DanceTrack, 76.0 on SportsMOT, and 71.1 IDF1 on PersonPath22. MOTIP2 is a family of models spanning the speed-accuracy trade-off: a lighter model, MOTIP2-S, matches the original MOTIP at over 3x the speed, and MOTIP2-X reaches 74.8 HOTA on DanceTrack.

title: Agentic AI-Assisted Modeling for Production Scheduling: Assessment in Constraint Programming
abstract: Developing optimization models for production scheduling requires substantial expert effort. Research on large language models (LLMs) has followed two directions: specialized approaches for automated modeling, mostly for mixed-integer linear programming, which often rely on dedicated training or problem-specific architectures that limit industrial deployment; and agentic artificial intelligence for operational decision support, which generally assumes that the optimization model already exists. This study bridges both directions by assessing whether general-purpose LLMs, orchestrated as agents without task-specific training, can formulate and implement constraint programming models from natural-language problem descriptions. Singleagent and multi-agent architectures are integrated with a Model Context Protocol server that provides context-aware retrieval of solver documentation to mitigate hallucinations during implementation. Both are compared with a direct LLM baseline on six industry-oriented problems covering flow-shop, job-shop, flexible job-shop and resource-constrained warehouse scheduling, using three LLMs and assessing modeling accuracy, execution success, latency and token consumption. Formulation proves largely within reach of current LLMs, whereas implementation is the main barrier. The multi-agent workflow raises the share of scripts that run correctly as generated from 14.8% with a direct LLM call to 59.3%, reaching 80.6% on the four less complex problems, while tightly coupled intralogistics models remain an open challenge.

title: Beyond Source-Level Transfer: Sample-Level Learning for High-Dimensional Quantile Regression
abstract: This paper studies transfer learning for high-dimensional quantile regression with limited target samples and heterogeneous source domains. We propose a sample-level transfer learning method (SL-TL) that combines sample selection and importance weighting. Unlike existing source-level approaches that include or exclude entire source domains, SL-TL identifies transferable samples within each source domain and incorporates them through adaptive importance weights. The proposed weights rely only on one-dimensional densities associated with the quantile loss, avoiding the estimation of high-dimensional density ratios. We establish error bounds for SL-TL estimators and characterize the effective sample size contributed by source domains. In the oracle setting, we show that SL-TL achieves faster $\ell_2$-convergence rates than existing competitors under the considered regimes. For the unknown setting, we develop an implementable algorithm based on sample splitting and cross-fitting procedures. Extensive simulations and a real data analysis demonstrate the finite-sample performance and robustness of SL-TL.

title: VeriSBOM: Secure and Verifiable SBOM Sharing via Zero-Knowledge Proofs
abstract: SBOMs often contain sensitive information that organizations are unwilling to disclose in full. To avoid disruption of privacy and confidentiality in delivering plaintext SBOMs, we present VeriSBOM, a trustless SBOM framework that provides cryptographic verifiability of SBOMs using zero-knowledge proofs, i.e., third-parties can validate if software contains authentic dependencies distributed by official package managers and that the same dependencies are compliant with policy constraints. The verification process requires no trust in the SBOM publisher beyond the soundness of the underlying primitives, and third parties can independently check proofs against the public cryptographic commitments. We design and implement VeriSBOM, analyze its security, evaluate its performance on real-world package registries and SBOMs, and evaluate its usability.

The verification process requires no trust in the SBOM publisher beyond the soundness of the underlying primitives, and third parties can independently check proofs against the public cryptographic commitments. We design and implement VeriSBOM, analyze its security, evaluate its performance on real-world package registries and SBOMs, and evaluate its usability.

title: A SIMULATION STUDY OF INDONESIAN SENTIMENT CLASSIFICATION FOR A WHATSAPP STUDENT SUPPORT CHATBOT
abstract: Short Indonesian messages may help institutions organise student support requests, but sentiment polarity does not directly measure psychological well-being. This study evaluates a text-classification component intended for a WhatsApp student support chatbot through a fully synthetic, reproducible simulation. A constructed corpus contains 360 messages from 60 scenario families across six support domains. Families, including their positive and negative variants, are separated into training, validation, and test partitions of 216, 72, and 72 messages. A further 48 synthetic messages test negation, abbreviations, language mixing, and explicitly mixed sentiment. Term frequency–inverse document frequency features and multinomial Naïve Bayes are compared with a constant baseline and logistic regression. On the held-out synthetic test set, Naïve Bayes achieves accuracy of 0.875 and macro-F1 of 0.875, matching logistic regression on both aggregate metrics. On the challenge set, its accuracy decreases to 0.813 and macro-F1 to 0.806. Negation is the weakest scenario, with six correct predictions out of twelve; all six positive negation examples are misclassified. Feature inspection links selected errors to polarity-bearing words and unseen abbreviations. The results establish a reproducible computational baseline and expose limitations obscured by aggregate scores. They do not validate real student conversations, live WhatsApp integration, stress detection, or improvements in well-being.

title: Hybrid Behaviour Tree–LLM Architectures for Latency-Sensitive Agent Control: A Preliminary Mapping Review, Taxonomy, and Implications for Real-Time Game AI
abstract: Agentic AI systems support contextual reasoning, long-horizon planning, and adaptive behaviour, but their use of large language models (LLMs) can introduce substantial latency that limits their suitability for immediate decision-making and highly responsive feedback in latency-sensitive real-time systems such as multiplayer combat games. In contrast, real-time game AI commonly employs low-latency symbolic controllers, including Behaviour Trees, Utility Systems, and Finite State Machines, which provide predictable and computationally efficient execution but offer more limited contextual reasoning and semantic flexibility. Emerging hybrid architectures seek to combine these properties by using LLMs for higher-level reasoning while retaining symbolic controllers for latency-sensitive execution. This review synthesizes current approaches to Behaviour Tree–LLM integration and examines their architectural characteristics for latency-sensitive real-time game AI. As an original contribution, we formalize an end-to-end latency model for decision processes and introduce four parameterised temporal regions for relating decision latency to engineering time budgets. We further develop a multidimensional taxonomy of hybrid BT–LLM architectures covering latency, adaptability, grounding, planning, and autonomy, together with cross-cutting LLM deployment characteristics. Across the reviewed literature, hybrid architectures commonly separate LLM-mediated deliberation from symbolic execution pathways, with LLMs contributing to strategic reasoning, planning, policy selection, contextual interpretation, and adaptation, while Behaviour Trees provide executable control.

title: Stability of energy-constrained bosonic capacities under extensions of LOCC
abstract: Abstract: The energy-constrained two-way capacities of pure-loss and quantum-limited amplifier channels have been determined in a combined treatment using finite-round local operations and classical communication with finite or countable outcomes. We prove that the same vanishing-error capacities hold when local instruments have standard Borel outcomes and measurable feedback, and when the classical protocol terminates almost surely without a deterministic bound on its number of rounds. We also specify limiting classes for which the converse remains valid. For quantum and private-state targets, normal strong limits of reduced LOCC channels are covered by complete preservation of separability. For operational secret key, the public realization must be retained: we construct local purifying shields for instruments whose faithful Choi densities factor at each public outcome, and prove an averaged replica bound without representing a continuous record as an orthogonal quantum register. These arguments preserve every transmitted input marginal and require no bound on local memory dimension, energy, or entropy. Energy-controlled limits of complete protocols provide a further extension. The results confirm both capacity formulas under these explicitly defined enlargements and identify why a reduced-map closure alone cannot define secret-key security.

title: CIPIHunter: Detecting Configuration-Induced Prediction Instability in Deep Learning Frameworks
abstract: Deep learning (DL) frameworks support diverse execution configurations, including precision modes and model optimizations. Even with a fixed model, input, and framework version, changing these configurations can change model predictions, causing Configuration-Induced Prediction Instability (CIPI). It arises when configuration-dependent numerical perturbations propagate and cause potentially harmful model-level behavior. Existing API-level and model-level testing approaches are not well suited to detecting CIPI, as these approaches lack configuration-conditioned exploration and propagation-aware diagnosis. Therefore, we present CIPIHunter, which combines controlled configuration-pair testing, sensitivity-oriented mutation, feedback-guided search, and intermediate tracing to localize suspicious operators or operator groups. On 13 PyTorch models under a 100-round budget, CIPIHunter reports the highest raw CIPI count and 22 deduplicated Type I manifestations, 83.3% more than the strongest baseline, while remaining competitive in overall deduplicated manifestation coverage. In total, we submit 29 PyTorch issue reports. Developers have acknowledged eight, rejected five, and marked four as duplicates; nine remain pending, and three have been closed without an explicit determination. Separately, three reports are labeled “high-priority”. These results demonstrate the practical utility of CIPI testing for framework quality assurance.

title: Dynamically protected erasure qubit via low-frequency charge driving
abstract: Dynamical protection via strong driving can enable resilient quantum processing on imperfect physical hardware. However, the practical utility of such schemes is frequently limited by parasitic processes such as drive-induced dephasing and leakage. Here, we demonstrate that sub-GHz charge driving of superconducting Kerr oscillators (KOs) in the transmon regime circumvents this trade-off, simultaneously activating fast parametric interactions and protecting the encoded qubit from low-frequency noise. The key is the frequency dependence of the charge sensitivity: using the AC Stark shift as a probe, we find that the KO frequency sensitivity to a charge drive grows quadratically with both drive frequency and amplitude, making the oscillator weakly sensitive to $1/f$ charge noise yet strongly coupled to drives near 1~GHz. Exploiting this, we first demonstrate cooling and reset of the KO in 82~ns, to a residual population below $0.7\%$---lower than its $2.5\%$ steady-state thermal population. Next, using two KOs, we demonstrate logical control and dynamical protection of a dual-rail qubit with nearly fourfold erasure bias. Finally, using a single end-of-circuit erasure check, we achieve an error per Clifford of $5.6\times10^{-4}$, which falls to $1.5\times10^{-4}$ after post-selection, with 25~ns gates.

title: Explicit Geometric Chain-of-Thought for Vision-Language-Action in Autonomous Driving
abstract: Vision-language-action~(VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for autonomous driving. However, existing VLA models still suffer from a fundamental mismatch: driving actions require precise 3D geometric cues, while visual-language understanding and reasoning are largely conducted in a 2D semantic space. In this paper, we propose GeoCoTDrive, an explicit geometric chain-of-thought framework that grounds geometry in a planning-oriented manner. GeoCoTDrive follows a think with 2D first, drive with dedicated 3D priors paradigm. It first grounds 2D regions corresponding to decision-critical cues, and then retrieves localized 3D priors by sampling features from a geometric foundation model within the grounded regions. These localized geometric features are interleaved into the autoregressive context to support the trajectory generation. To supervise this process, we introduce planning-relevant grounding, a new region-level grounding task that focuses on local spatial cues directly affecting ego planning decisions, and construct the PlanningGrounding dataset to endow VLAs with planning-oriented grounding capability. Experiments across multiple end-to-end autonomous driving benchmarks show that GeoCoTDrive consistently improves safety-critical planning performance, demonstrating the effectiveness of the explicit geometric chain-of-thought process for VLA-based planning.

title: VideoEvolve: Co-Evolving Memory and Retrieval for Long Video Understanding
abstract: Long video understanding increasingly relies on external memory to organize massive visual streams into compact representations. However, most memory-based methods dynamically adapt how information is retrieved for different questions, while largely fixing what is remembered. This mismatch makes missing details costly to recover, whereas stored information is valuable only when it can be reliably retrieved. To address this issue, we propose VideoEvolve, a novel self-evolving framework that jointly evolves memory and retrieval for long video understanding. Specifically, starting from a coarse low-frame-rate overview, VideoEvolve couples a Memory Evolver for selective memory augmentation with a Retrieval Evolver for adaptive retrieval over the evolving memory. We then co-evolve the two Evolvers through alternating agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL), updating one while freezing the other. To steer this alternating evolution, Bottleneck-Aware Evolution Feedback (BEF) identifies whether the current bottleneck lies in memory or retrieval and directs optimization toward the more limiting side. Furthermore, VideoEvolve introduces Capability-Aware Evolution Feedback (CEF) to alleviate downstream feedback from over-specializing memory to a fixed set of training questions, shifting training toward underdeveloped yet learnable video capabilities. By integrating Agentic RL with BEF and CEF, VideoEvolve transforms downstream reasoning experience into transferable capability updates, providing a concrete path from static long-video systems toward experience-driven, self-improving multimodal intelligence. Extensive experiments on multiple long video understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of VideoEvolve.

title: Learning joint probabilistic weather forecasts from station observations alone
abstract: Assessing compound weather risks requires forecasts representing dependence between variables. CLARA (Calibrated Advection-Routing Attention) learns joint Gaussian predictive distributions of five surface variables from station observations alone, without numerical weather prediction or reanalysis; the approximately 28,000-parameter model supports CPU training and prediction. Across six multi-year folds on 96 stations, its lead-mean energy score is 4.9% lower than that of a learned comparator with matched temporal inputs (4.7% with a similar parameter count) and 11-65% lower than those of statistical baselines. Holding marginal variances fixed, removing learned correlations worsens joint negative log-likelihood by 1.0-2.8 nats per station. A covariance-scale estimator, proved consistent under stated assumptions, improves short-lead calibration but over-corrects at long leads. Synthetic interventions show an attention-bias coefficient alone does not measure forecast influence. Retrained in ten regions on six continents, CLARA outperforms persistence in all 60 multi-year region-lead comparisons and a similarly sized learned model in 57 of 60.

title: LLM-Enabled UAV Dispatch: A System-Level Survey and Taxonomy
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) dispatch is beginning to move beyond isolated path planning and optimization-driven resource allocation toward system-level coordination supported by semantic reasoning and LLM-based interfaces. This survey provides a unified characterization of LLM-enabled UAV dispatch systems that bridges semantic intent, symbolic decision-making, and physical UAV execution. Rather than treating LLMs as standalone add-ons, we conceptualize them as a cross-layer semantic orchestration layer connecting human instructions, external solvers, and distributed control modules. We organize the literature into four representative dispatch paradigms: pipeline dispatch, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch. For each paradigm, we analyze its decision logic, system structure, control flow, representative methods, and potential LLM roles. We further examine how LLMs support semantic parsing, retrieval-grounded planning, solver orchestration, local agent reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety assessment, and human-facing explanation. We discuss the implications of these paradigms for scalability, robustness, coordination burden, and verification requirements, and identify open challenges including latency-aware reasoning, grounding reliability, physical feasibility guarantees, edge deployment, privacy protection, and distributed consistency. This survey provides a system-level taxonomy and design perspective for integrating LLMs into safety-critical UAV dispatch systems.

title: The genomic topological operator: a model for strong AI
abstract: The proposed “Genomic Topological Operator” (GTO) computing system architecture is inspired by the dynamic 3D organization of the genome in neurons. Unlike neural networks, the GTO relies on a biologically inspired genome architecture that fosters self-organization through a closed C1–C2 loop and plasticity. Its implementation is governed by physical principles: stochasticity, locality, and a hierarchy of time scales. The system comprises two layers on a unified substrate: a conservative C1 layer (analogous to the body) and a plastic C2 layer (analogous to the mind). C2 is isolated from external signals, receiving only integrated information from C1. Within C2, self-reference emerges through the construction of an internal self-model and autonomous structural modification. The model is presented in two versions: a basic version (featuring fixed clusters and weights, serving as a proof-of-concept) and an extended version (incorporating dynamic clustering and connection plasticity to enable self-organization). The model draws on actual biological data (Hi-C, RNA-seq, WGBS, etc.) and is empirically testable. The goal of this work is to create self-organizing computing systems for AGI.

title: Reproducibility archive for Loop-Phase Chirality in Matched Quantum-State Discrimination with an Exact Calibration Frontier
abstract: Reproducibility archive supporting the manuscript “Loop-Phase Chirality in Matched Quantum-State Discrimination with an Exact Calibration Frontier” by Matthias Jakob. The archive contains the Python numerical-audit and calibration-frontier verification scripts, pinned package requirements, machine-readable numerical tables, retained paired synthetic device draws, verification reports, figure generators, and supplementary material in PDF and LaTeX formats. The ideal discrimination optima and cancellation results are analytic. The numerical tolerance results are synthetic and use the residual ensemble specified in the manuscript and supplementary material. No experimental data were created or analyzed. The audit evaluates the full Born count model, including an imperfect binary switch and the strength-dependent detected-count denominator. See the included README for execution instructions, model conventions, provenance, seeds, and limitations. The archive supports reproducibility of the reported numerical checks; it does not constitute experimental validation. Deposition does not imply journal acceptance or peer-review approval.

title: Self-consistent entanglement certification and its complexity.
abstract: Conventional entanglement witnesses and quantum state tomography can, in principle, certify any entangled state but require prior characterization of the measurement devices. Bell tests remove this requirement but certify only those entangled states that are Bell nonlocal. In this talk, I will present a self-consistent alternative to entanglement certification. This approach uses experimentally inferred operational identities to certify entanglement through of the violation of noncontextuality inequalities, it requires no prior characterization of measurement devices and can, in principle, certify any entangled state. Finally, I will briefly discuss the complexity of self-consistent entanglement certification and its implications for developing practical self-consistent certification methods beyond entanglement.

title: MiniPoly: Automatic Extraction of Efficient JavaScript Polyfill from Language Specification
abstract: A polyfill is a JavaScript implementation of built-in APIs for older execution environments lacking native support. Because developers rely on them to run modern features everywhere, strict conformity to the official language specification (ECMA-262) is crucial. However, manual implementation remains the industry standard; this process is labor-intensive, inherently error-prone, and frequently leads to spec-miscompliance bugs in production.
